query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) to single-phase ZrB2 ceramic can lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
generation.conditions: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1600 °C for 10 min under a uniaxial load of 30 MPa
generation.mechanism: Improved mechanical properties due to enhanced densification, fine grains, and dispersion of CNTs
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased relative density, hardness, flexural strength, and fracture toughness
generation.baseline: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 ceramic prepared at temperatures above 2300 °C
generation.boundary: Preparation temperature below 2300 °C, exposure to liquid plating bath
generation.uncertainty: Optimal CNT content and sintering conditions for maximum mechanical properties

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled preparation and testing of single-phase ZrB2 ceramic with and without CNTs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of CNTs does not result in improved mechanical properties, the hypothesis is falsified

urces for the preparation of nanograined ZrB2 ceramics have been developed in the last decades.
To prepare nanostructured ZrB2-based ceramics, nanoscale powder and rapid sintering processes are required to inhibit abnormal grain growth during the sintering process. In this respect, the conventional sintering techniques (hot pressing, pressureless sintering, etc.) are quite challenging, due to the high temperatures and long dwelling times involved that lead to considerable grain coarsening in the product [,]. By employing a pulsed direct current (DC) current to improve sintering kinetics, spark plasma sintering (SPS) has emerged as a promising approach for densifying a number of poorly sinterable ceramics at a lower temperature and in a shorter time, while preserving an ultra-fine grain size [,,]. Previous studies on ZrB2-based ceramic materials showed that SPS enhanced densification and refined the microstructure in very short processing cycles [,]. However, the unsatisfactory value of the toughness still is an obstacle for the wide use of ZrB2-based ceramics, especially for applications in severe environments. The authors reported fracture toughness values of up to 6.9 MPa·m1/2 for the composites compared with the value of 3.5 MPa·m1/2 for the monolithic alumina. To date, there have been fewer reports on CNTs toughening ZrB2-based ceramics. Tian and Lin et al. [,] reported that the addition of CNTs produced promising results. For instance, for ZrB2-based composites, fracture toughness values up to 5.6–7.2 MPa·m1/2 were reported.
In this paper, CNTs were chosen as the reinforcement. Nanograined ZrB2 ceramics with and without the addition of CNTs were fabricated by SPS. For comparison, coarse-grained ZrB2-CNTs composites were also sintered by SPS. The microstructure and mechanical properties of the composites were investigated.
